query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys, particularly CrMnFeCoNi, high-temperature structural and chemical stability is compromised primarily by the preferential oxidation of Mn driven by enhanced grain boundary diffusion, which overrides the sluggish kinetic diffusion benefit of the high entropy effect.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy nanoalloy with a homogeneous microstructure and typical nano-scale grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to high-temperature oxidative environments (e.g., air and vacuum) and compare standard processed samples with those subjected to grain boundary engineering (to modify diffusion paths).
generation.conditions: Temperatures above 800 °C under both atmospheric and vacuum conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary diffusion dynamics that facilitate faster transport of Mn relative to other elements.
generation.mechanism: Although high-entropy alloys are designed for sluggish diffusion and chemical stability, Mn exhibits relatively higher mobility along grain boundaries at elevated temperatures. Its preferential oxidation forms non-protective Mn-rich oxides, which deplete Mn from the bulk alloy and undermine both the structural integrity and chemical stability of the nanoalloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Standard nanoalloy samples will display significant Mn depletion and the formation of non-protective Mn oxides, especially in oxygen-rich environments. In contrast, samples with engineered grain boundaries (which slow Mn diffusion) will exhibit reduced oxide formation and better retention of Mn, leading to improved stability.
generation.baseline: Standard equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy nanoalloy processed without grain boundary modifications under identical high-temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds for nanoalloys with similar equiatomic compositions and nano-scale grain structures; results may vary for different compositions, phase segregations, or if other elements unexpectedly dominate diffusion under altered processing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The relative activation energies for Mn diffusion versus other elements at nano-scale grain boundaries and the extent to which grain boundary engineering can mitigate Mn oxidation are not fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi nanoalloys: one set with standard processing and another set where grain boundaries are engineered (e.g., via dopants or thermo-mechanical treatments to reduce grain boundary area or modify its properties). Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., >800 °C) under identical atmospheric conditions (air) and monitor the oxidation evolution in real time using in situ XRD combined with post-mortem elemental mapping techniques.
measurements: Rate and extent of Mn oxide formation via XRD phase analysis
Elemental distribution profiles (especially of Mn) using techniques like EDS or SIMS
Thickness and composition of oxide scales
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered grain boundary sample does not show a statistically significant reduction in Mn oxide formation and Mn depletion compared to the standard sample, or if both samples show similar oxidation behaviors, then the hypothesis that Mn's enhanced grain boundary diffusion governs instability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
